title: Gonococcal septic arthritis: gram-negative intracellular diplococci
vignette: A 22-year-old sexually active woman comes to the emergency department due to 2 days of severe right knee pain and swelling. She takes oral contraceptive pills and reports several new sexual partners over the past month. Temperature is 38.5 C (101.3 F). The right knee is warm, erythematous, and markedly swollen with painful, limited range of motion, and a few pustular skin lesions are noted on the distal extremities. Arthrocentesis yields cloudy synovial fluid with a leukocyte count of 50,000/mm3 (normal <200), predominantly neutrophils. Which of the following is most likely seen on Gram stain of the joint fluid?

clues.note: A young, sexually active adult is the classic host for gonococcal arthritis, the most common cause of septic arthritis in this group.

clues.text: several new sexual partners over the past month
clues.note: Multiple new partners is the key risk factor pointing to Neisseria gonorrhoeae as the pathogen.

clues.text: pustular skin lesions are noted on the distal extremities
clues.note: Pustular skin lesions accompanying arthritis indicate disseminated gonococcal infection (arthritis-dermatitis syndrome).
Synovial WBC ~50,000 / normal <200 with neutrophil predominance confirms bacterial (septic) arthritis, a joint-threatening emergency.

whatMatters: A sexually active young adult with acute monoarticular septic arthritis (synovial WBC ~50,000) plus pustular skin lesions = disseminated gonococcal infection. On Gram stain, Neisseria gonorrhoeae appears as GRAM-NEGATIVE INTRACELLULAR DIPLOCOCCI (within neutrophils). Answer A.
strategy: Combine the demographic (young, sexually active, new partners) with septic arthritis + pustules to reach gonococcus, then recall its Gram-stain morphology: gram-negative diplococci, often inside neutrophils. Reject gram-positive clusters (S. aureus - the most common overall, but less likely with this sexual history + pustules), chains (streptococci), and gram-negative rods.

eliminations.label: Gram-positive cocci in clusters - Staphylococcus aureus
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: S. aureus, the most common cause of septic arthritis overall. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the sexual history plus pustular dermatitis point to gonococcus in this young patient; S. aureus lacks the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome. ✅ Correct if: septic arthritis after skin breach/IV drug use without STI features.

eliminations.label: Gram-positive cocci in chains - streptococci
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: streptococci (e.g., group A/B). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: they can cause septic arthritis but don't fit the gonococcal arthritis-dermatitis picture with pustules and new partners. ✅ Correct if: streptococcal septic arthritis (often with a skin/soft-tissue source).

eliminations.label: Gram-negative rods - wrong morphology/host
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: gram-negative bacilli (e.g., E. coli, Pseudomonas). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: these cause septic arthritis mainly in neonates, elderly, or IV drug users - not this young, otherwise healthy woman with STI risk. ✅ Correct if: septic arthritis in a neonate/immunocompromised host or IV drug user (Pseudomonas).

eliminations.label: Gram-positive rods - not a typical septic-arthritis pattern
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: gram-positive bacilli (e.g., Listeria, Bacillus). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: not the causative morphology here; gonococcus is a gram-negative diplococcus. ✅ Correct if: a Listeria/Bacillus scenario, not gonococcal arthritis.

reasoning: Young sexually active woman + acute septic knee (WBC 50,000) + pustular skin lesions = disseminated gonococcal infection
N. gonorrhoeae is the classic cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults
Its Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci, characteristically within neutrophils
mechanism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus (kidney-bean-shaped pairs) that is often seen INSIDE neutrophils on Gram stain (intracellular diplococci). After mucosal infection, it can disseminate hematogenously to cause the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome (migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and pustular skin lesions) or a purulent monoarticular septic arthritis, as in this patient's knee (synovial WBC ~50,000/mm3 with neutrophil predominance). Gonococcus is fastidious and grows on chocolate (Thayer-Martin) agar; joint-fluid cultures are frequently negative, so nucleic acid amplification testing of genital specimens supports the diagnosis. Risk is highest in sexually active young adults with new/multiple partners; terminal complement (C5-C9) deficiency predisposes to dissemination. Septic arthritis is a joint-destroying emergency requiring prompt drainage and antibiotics (ceftriaxone).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: S. aureus (gram-positive clusters) is #1 overall but the sexual history + pustules favor gonococcus; chains = strep; gram-negative rods = neonate/elderly/IVDU.

difficulty.message: Bank: gonococcal arthritis -> gram-negative intracellular diplococci; treat ceftriaxone + drainage; check complement if recurrent.
